examples: There is a cow on the farm.
nuance: 소 is the animal cow or ox. Its meat is 소고기 (or 쇠고기), a separate word, so do not use 소 when you mean beef. Because 소 ends in a vowel it takes 가, and like other animals it is counted with 마리.
mistakes: Saying 소 when you mean beef — that is 소고기.
Counting cows with 개 instead of 마리; say 소 한 마리.

examples: There is a mouse in the kitchen.
nuance: 쥐 covers both mouse and rat; Korean does not split the two the way English does. It is one syllable and ends in a vowel, so use 쥐가. A computer mouse is the loanword 마우스, not 쥐.
mistakes: Calling a computer mouse 쥐 — that is 마우스.
Counting mice with 개; animals take 마리, so 쥐 한 마리.

examples: I saw a snake on the mountain.
nuance: 뱀 is a snake. It ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes the subject marker 이 (뱀이) and the object marker 을 (뱀을). It is counted with 마리 like other animals.
mistakes: Saying 뱀가 있어요 — after a consonant use 이, so 뱀이 있어요.
Counting snakes with 개; use 마리, so 뱀 한 마리.

examples: There are many frogs in the rice paddy.
nuance: 개구리 is a frog. The sound a frog makes uses the verb 울다 (to cry), the same verb used for many animal sounds, so 개구리가 울어요 means the frog croaks. A tadpole is 올챙이, a separate word.
mistakes: Saying 개구리가 노래해요 for its sound; animal cries use 울다.
Dropping a syllable and writing 개구 instead of 개구리.

examples: There is a bug in the room.
nuance: 벌레 is the everyday general word for a bug, insect, or worm. It is broader than 곤충, which is the scientific term 'insect'. For tiny creatures Koreans still use the counter 마리, so 벌레 한 마리.
mistakes: Using the formal 곤충 in casual speech where 벌레 is natural.
Counting bugs with 개; small creatures take 마리, so 벌레 한 마리.

usage: I got bitten by a mosquito
examples: There are many mosquitoes in summer.
I got bitten by a mosquito so it itches.
nuance: 모기 is a mosquito. To say you were bitten, the natural phrase is 모기에 물렸어요, using the passive 물리다 with the particle 에. Mosquitoes are a common summer complaint, so this phrase comes up often.
mistakes: Saying 모기가 물렸어요 for being bitten — use 모기에 물렸어요.
Counting mosquitoes with 개; use 마리, so 모기 한 마리.

examples: A butterfly landed on the flower.
There are many butterflies in the garden.
nuance: 나비 is a butterfly. It ends in a vowel, so it takes 가. The verb for flying is 날다, and for landing on a flower Koreans use 앉다 (to sit). A moth is 나방, a different word.
mistakes: Confusing 나비 (butterfly) with 나방 (moth).
Counting butterflies with 개; small creatures take 마리, so 나비 한 마리.

examples: There is a spider on the ceiling.
One spider is on the wall.
nuance: 거미 is a spider. Its web is 거미줄, a compound of 거미 + 줄 (line/thread). Like other small creatures it is counted with 마리, and it ends in a vowel so it takes 가.
mistakes: Calling the web 거미 — the web is 거미줄.
Counting spiders with 개; use 마리, so 거미 한 마리.

examples: The child sat on the ground.
The land here is really wide.
I dug the ground and planted a tree.
nuance: 땅 means the ground, land, or soil under our feet. It ends in the consonant ㅇ, so it takes 이 (땅이). For the planet Earth Koreans say 지구, not 땅, so keep the two ideas separate.
mistakes: Saying 땅가 넓어요 — after a consonant use 이, so 땅이 넓어요.
Using 땅 for the planet Earth; that is 지구.

usage: I put out the fire / turn off the light
examples: The room is dark. I turn on the light.
A fire broke out in the kitchen.
nuance: 불 means fire, but it also means the light of a lamp, so 불을 켜다 / 불을 끄다 means to turn a light on/off. It ends in ㄹ, so it takes 이 (불이). To say a fire breaks out, use the set phrase 불이 나다.
mistakes: Saying 불가 났어요 — after a consonant use 이, so 불이 났어요.
Using 열다/닫다 for a light; lights and fire use 켜다 (on) and 끄다 (off).

examples: The mountain air is really fresh.
I opened the window and breathed the air.
nuance: 공기 is the air we breathe. For fresh air Koreans say 공기가 맑다 (clear), and for fresh air to breathe you can use 마시다 (literally drink/inhale). For air pollution specifically, the related word is 미세먼지 (fine dust).
mistakes: Confusing 공기 (air) with 날씨 (weather); they are different ideas.
Saying 공기가 깨끗하다 is fine, but the more natural set phrase for air is 공기가 맑다.

examples: I eat an orange in the morning.
One glass of orange juice, please.
nuance: 오렌지 is the imported orange and a loanword from English. The native Korean citrus 귤 (tangerine/mandarin) is smaller and far more common in homes, so do not mix the two. Count whole fruit with 개: 오렌지 한 개.
mistakes: Confusing 오렌지 (orange) with 귤 (tangerine/mandarin).
Counting fruit with 마리; fruit uses 개, so 오렌지 한 개.

examples: This chili pepper is too spicy.
I added chili peppers to the stew.
I make kimchi with chili powder.
nuance: 고추 is the chili pepper, a key ingredient in Korean cooking. Ground into powder it becomes 고춧가루 (note the 사이시옷, the inserted ㅅ), and the red chili paste is 고추장. A green chili is 풋고추.
mistakes: Writing the powder as 고추가루; the standard spelling is 고춧가루.
Confusing 고추 (chili pepper) with 후추 (black pepper).

usage: I watch a movie at the cinema
examples: I go to the cinema on weekends.
I watched a movie at the theater.
Let's meet in front of the theater.
nuance: 극장 is a movie theater or cinema, and also a theater for live performances. In daily speech many people say 영화관 specifically for movie theaters, but 극장 is the common older word and is widely understood. Use 에 to go there and 에서 for watching a film.
mistakes: Saying 극장에서 가요 for going there — use 극장에 가요.
Saying 극장가 커요 — after a consonant use 이, so 극장이 커요.

usage: I buy books at the bookstore
examples: I bought a book at the bookstore.
There is a bookstore near the school.
Do you want to go to the bookstore together?
nuance: 서점 is a bookstore. It ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes 이 (서점이). Use 에 to go there and 에서 to buy books there. A library, where you borrow books, is 도서관 — a different place.
mistakes: Confusing 서점 (bookstore, you buy) with 도서관 (library, you borrow).
Saying 서점가 있어요 — after a consonant use 이, so 서점이 있어요.

usage: I go to the hair salon
I get my hair cut at the salon
examples: I'm going to the hair salon tomorrow.
I got my hair cut at the salon.
There is a hair salon in front of my house.
nuance: 미용실 is a hair/beauty salon, where you cut, dye, or perm your hair. A barbershop for men is 이발소, a more old-fashioned place; many people of all genders now just use 미용실 or the loanword 헤어숍. Use 머리를 자르다 for getting a haircut.
mistakes: Confusing 미용실 (hair salon) with 이발소 (traditional barbershop).
Saying 미용실가 있어요 — after a consonant use 이, so 미용실이 있어요.
